content.p: The Latin Kings are a street gang that has been the target of many federal prosecutions. Federal prosecutors in Chicago, Indiana, Maryland, New York and Massachusetts have each described the group, in indictments and press releases, as a racketeering enterprise with a chain of command, written rules and an internal system of punishment. Its members, in the same documents, are accused of drug dealing, shootings and murder.

The gang is also an unusual one. It began, according to the accounts that survive, as a group meant to protect Puerto Rican immigrants in Chicago, and by the 1980s a manifesto, written by a man in prison for murder, laid out what it meant to be a Latin King. For a period in the late 1990s one New York leader tried to turn it into something other than a gang. Most of the court record, however, concerns what came after: leaders sentenced to decades in prison, a Chicago police officer who pleaded guilty to working with the gang, and a series of killings that prosecutors tied to its discipline.
Everything below about a person who has been charged but not convicted is an allegation. Prosecutors' press releases state that an indictment is not a finding of guilt.

There is no agreed founding date. The US Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of New York, in a 2007 press release, says the Latin Kings originated in Chicago in the 1940s. The public radio programme Latino USA says they started in the 1950s, and describes their original aim as shielding Puerto Rican immigrants from racist attacks and discrimination. Over time, it says, the gang "morphed into a criminal enterprise".

A third account comes from a Chicago gang-history website that credits two men, "King Rory" and "King Phil", with the foundation, with Phil as the founder. It says Phil arrived in Chicago from Puerto Rico in 1952 and settled on the Near West Side. In 1958 he moved to the Eckhart Park area, where he joined a club called the Aces. The site says the Aces were outnumbered and losing a fight with mostly white gangs, and that Phil renamed the club the Skulls to frighten rivals and attract recruits. The site itself speaks of "many legends" about the founding, and its author hedges parts of the story with phrases such as "I am not sure" and "I believe". It also describes a separate Laflin and Van Buren group of Latin Kings that, it says, merged with the Almighty Latin Kings in the late 1960s.

The same website describes the Chicago of the late 1950s as a patchwork of hostile neighbourhoods. Eckhart Park, it says, sat on the border between Italian, Polish, Irish, Mexican and Ukrainian areas, and the construction of the Dan Ryan Expressway in 1958 displaced many Hispanic and African American families and pushed Puerto Ricans into Eckhart Park and Humboldt Park. They were not welcomed, it says, and endured racial conflict.

The website's account of the group's growth in the 1960s is detailed but its author hedges it. It says the "Boulevards" branch of the Latin Kings was established in about May 1966, when a leader known as Don Juan went to the Little Village neighbourhood, and that the Little Village group took in many white members. According to the site, almost half of the Latin Kings outside 24th and Marshall were white in the 1960s because the community stayed majority white into the 1970s. The same author says a Cicero chapter formed in 1966 and went defunct in the early 1970s. These are the website's claims, not findings of a court.
content.h2: Luis Felipe and the New York offshoot
content.p: The gang's identity changed in the 1980s partly in a prison rather than on a Chicago street. The Eastern District of New York dates the gang's arrival in New York City to the 1980s and ties it to a tribe set up inside a prison in the north of the state. Separately, Latino USA names Luis Felipe, known as "King Blood", as a man who by the 1980s was "running the show" while in prison for murder; it does not say he formed that tribe. Felipe, it says, taught young Latino inmates that Latinos were strong and ought to take pride in their heritage, and he wrote a manifesto laying out what being a Latin King meant.

One man who absorbed that message was Antonio Fernandez, a man from East New York who was then serving time at Riker’s Island. Latino USA says he was so taken by Felipe and the manifesto that after his release he resolved to change the organisation from within. His aim, according to the programme, was to make the Kings give up violence and drug dealing and instead oppose what he saw as the oppression of Latinos. To do that he would have to take on the police, the FBI and the criminal justice system, and also his fellow Kings. He became known as "King Tone". Latino USA describes the late 1990s as a period in which he turned the gang into "a non-violent street organization".

Fernandez's reform did not end the matter. In 2007 a federal jury in Brooklyn convicted a man named Carlos Gil, a "Warlord" or enforcer of a Latin Kings chapter in Sunset Park, of the 2001 murder of 21-year-old Jorge Rodriguez. The evidence at trial, according to the US Attorney, was that Gil learned Rodriguez, a member of the Flatbush tribe, was associating with another gang in violation of the Kings' rules. A Flatbush member who was present refused Gil's order to kill Rodriguez, and Gil then gave a gun to a junior member of the Sunset Park tribe, aged 16, who shot Rodriguez dead on Gil's command. The teenager pleaded guilty and testified against Gil. The jury found that the Latin Kings were a racketeering enterprise and that the killing was carried out in furtherance of its racketeering activities. Judge Frederic Block sentenced Gil to life without the possibility of parole. By then, the US Attorney said, the gang had tribes in all five boroughs of New York City and on Long Island.

In Connecticut, a 1993 killing opened a feud that lasted more than a year. On 31 August 1993, at about 9 p.m., Felipe "Pipe" Santana, a 23-year-old member of the rival Los Solidos, was shot dead at the corner of Park and Wadsworth streets in Hartford. About half an hour later, Antonio Torres, 21, a reputed Latin King, was shot in the head at 98 Wadsworth Street. A prosecutor, Kevin Murphy, said the Santana murder was "the beginning of an escalating gang war" that led to the deaths of many people.

In August 1997 a Hartford man, Ralph Torres, 23, a reputed Latin King, was sentenced to 60 years in prison after being convicted of shooting Santana. He told the court that he was sorry for the family's loss but "did not do it", and his family said the real killer was still free. The case had rested on witnesses, many of them reluctant. The first trial ended with a deadlocked jury; the Courant reported that eight of its 12 members reportedly favoured acquittal. In the second trial the judge allowed a signed statement from a jailed Latin King that Torres had admitted the killing. The defence challenged the credibility of two convicted gang members who testified for the state in the hope of leniency. The judge said he would have reversed the verdict had he thought Torres innocent, and the family said it had hired a lawyer to appeal.

One of the main cases against the gang in its home city came out of investigations that began in the mid-2000s. According to the FBI, ATF agents led an investigation in late 2006 that produced federal drug and firearms charges against 38 members and associates. In 2008 an FBI-led investigation produced state and federal charges against 40 more. In total, more than 80 members and associates faced state or federal charges after 2006.

The central case was a racketeering indictment returned in September 2008, with a superseding indictment in October 2009, against 31 co-defendants. Of those, 24 pleaded guilty, four were convicted at trial and three remained fugitives. At the trial, which lasted five weeks, the jury found four men guilty in April 2011. The FBI describes the charge as running a criminal enterprise for personal enrichment, defending its power, territory and revenue through acts that included murder, attempted murder, extortion and armed assault.

The four were Augustin Zambrano, the "Corona", or national leader; Vicente Garcia Jr., the "Supreme Regional Inca", who prosecutors said oversaw the day-to-day illegal activity of all factions with some 10,000 members in Illinois alone; Jose Guzman, a former "Nation Enforcer" in the Little Village faction; and Alphonso Chavez, the "Inca" of the 31st and Drake faction. Zambrano was sentenced to 60 years in January 2012. Guzman received 35 years and Chavez 30. Fernando King, who preceded Garcia as Supreme Regional Inca and pleaded guilty, got 40 years in October 2011. In 2013 Judge Charles Norgle sentenced Garcia, known as "DK" or "Disciple Killer", to 40 years; he must serve at least 85 percent.

The evidence at the trial included audio and video recordings of three beatings inflicted on gang members for breaking rules, and testimony about three murders and 20 shootings in Little Village. According to the FBI, Garcia and Zambrano ranked higher than any Latin Kings convicted and sentenced since Gustavo "Gino" Colon, another Corona, received a life sentence in 2000. Gary Shapiro, the US Attorney, said the sentence held Garcia accountable for "the barbaric enterprise known as the Latin Kings".
content.h2: Indiana: murders, missions and a police officer
content.p: A second federal case, in the Northern District of Indiana, drew in Latin Kings from the Chicago area and from Indiana towns such as East Chicago and Hammond. A third superseding indictment, returned on 16 November 2011 and unsealed two days later, charged 21 defendants, and 23 members and associates were indicted in all. The indictments alleged that rules were enforced through murder, attempted murder and threats against anyone who broke them or threatened the gang, and that members had to obey superiors, including by carrying out "missions". The charges held the gang responsible for more than 20 murders.

One mission was described in a guilty plea. Jason Ortiz admitted that on 25 February 2007 he and four other defendants, armed with three firearms, travelled from Illinois to Griffith, Indiana, and were ordered to ambush rival gang members at a party. After two members of the Latin Dragons, James Walsh and Gonzalo Diaz, left the party, two of Ortiz's co-defendants got out of a vehicle and shot them dead. Ortiz was sentenced to 25 years. Another defendant, Jermaine Ellis, who the release says joined at an early age, admitted that as a juvenile he took part in the shootings and received more than 17 years.

The case also touched the Chicago Police Department. Alex Guerrero, a Chicago police officer, pleaded guilty to racketeering conspiracy, a drug conspiracy involving cocaine and marijuana, interference with commerce by threats or violence, and a firearms count; he admitted he was responsible for 150 kilograms or more of cocaine and had abused a position of public trust. His plea agreement set a 19-year sentence as appropriate. Another former officer, Antonio Martinez Jr., was sentenced to 12 years after pleading guilty. According to court records cited in the ICE release, he and a colleague committed armed robberies on behalf of a Latin Kings member, sometimes in uniform and in police vehicles, stealing drugs, weapons and cash. In May 2013 six defendants were sentenced in the case, including Martin Anaya, who received 30 years after a jury verdict.

The gang's reach was shown again in November 2009, when a federal grand jury in Greenbelt, Maryland, indicted 19 alleged members for conspiring to take part in a racketeering enterprise. The indictment alleged that the Latin Kings had been in Maryland since at least 2007, and that two men, Miguel Cruz and Erick Roman, established the "Royal Lion Tribe of Maryland" in the spring of that year. Prosecutors alleged attempted murders, robberies, witness tampering and arson, and that members hunted for rivals from MS-13. The document also described the gang's culture: crown-shaped hand-signs, the greeting "Amor De Rey", the colours black and gold, and organisation into "tribes". It stated that an indictment is not a finding of guilt.

A decade later the focus was Massachusetts. A federal grand jury returned an indictment in December 2019 against 62 leaders, members and associates of the Latin Kings, alleging racketeering and drug conspiracy and firearms offences. Court documents described a national manifesto, an internal judiciary and a hierarchy kept alive by a sophisticated communications system. One of the group's internal "trials", held in March 2019, was captured on video: it concerned Angel Roldan, the former second-in-command, or "Cacique", in Massachusetts, who reportedly stole drugs from fellow members and had not repaid drug debts to the New Bedford chapter's leader. Roldan pleaded guilty, and in July 2021 he was given seven years.

In January 2022 Esther Ortiz, 50, known as "Queen India", who sat on the Regional Crown Council and heard evidence about manifesto violations, was sentenced to time served, about 72 days, and three years of supervised release, after pleading guilty in October 2021. The government had recommended 21 months. She was the 42nd defendant sentenced in the case.
